paragraphs.heading: Silica with water in it
paragraphs.text: Opal is a hydrated, amorphous form of silica. By weight, water can make up anywhere from 3% to 21% of it, though the usual figure is between 6% and 10%. Because its structure is amorphous, opal is classed as a mineraloid. The crystalline forms of silica, by contrast, are considered minerals.

paragraphs.heading: Precious and common
paragraphs.text: Opal is deposited at a relatively low temperature and can turn up in fissures in almost any kind of rock. There are two broad classes. Precious opal shows play-of-color, flashes of colored light that appear as the stone is turned in white light; common opal does not. Depending on the conditions it formed in, opal can be transparent, translucent or opaque, and its background can be white, black or almost any color in the visual spectrum. The most common opals are white, gray and green, and black opal is considered the rarest.

paragraphs.heading: Tiny spheres in rows
paragraphs.text: Although it is a mineraloid, precious opal has an internal structure. At microscopic scales it is made of silica spheres some 150–300 nm in diameter, packed in a hexagonal or cubic close-packed lattice. These ordered spheres produce the internal colors by causing interference and diffraction of the light that passes through. How regular the spheres are in size and in packing is a prime factor in the quality of precious opal.

paragraphs.heading: How spacing picks the color
paragraphs.text: The stacked planes of spheres act as a grating. Where the gap between the planes is around half the wavelength of one component of visible light, light of that wavelength may be diffracted. The colors seen depend on the spacing between the planes and on how the planes are oriented relative to the incoming light. Bragg's law of diffraction describes the process.

paragraphs.heading: Cut stones and doublets
paragraphs.text: For jewellery, most opal is cut and polished into a cabochon, a convex shape that maximises the angles from which the play-of-color can be seen. A "natural" opal is a polished stone made wholly of precious opal. Opal too thin for that may be combined with other materials into a "composite" gem. An opal doublet is a fairly thin layer of precious opal with a backing of dark material, most often ironstone, dark or black common opal, onyx or obsidian. The darker backing emphasizes the play-of-color.

paragraphs.heading: Triplets
paragraphs.text: An opal triplet is like a doublet with one more layer on top, a domed cap made of clear quartz or plastic. The cap takes a high polish and protects the opal. It also works as a magnifier, emphasizing the play-of-color of the opal underneath, and that opal is often an inferior specimen or a very thin section of precious opal. Triplets tend to look more artificial and are classed as "composite" gemstones, not precious ones. A doublet, unlike a triplet, has genuine opal as its top layer, the one you see and touch.

paragraphs.heading: A word with two meanings
paragraphs.text: The term opalescence is commonly used for play-of-color. In gemology, though, opalescence means the hazy, milky sheen of common opal, which does not show a play of color. Precious opal's uses in jewelry can be somewhat limited: it is sensitive to heat, mainly because of its relatively high water content, and it is prone to scratching.
